title: Fix or quarantine the flaky SynchronousIoCancelTests
how_to_read: Each attempt is one line and a `details` filename in this same directory. Open a detail file ONLY when this index points you at one -- the summaries are here so you do not have to. `caused_by` is what sent the stage back; `changed` is what the attempt then touched, counted by kind. Several attempts in a row that were caused by the same stage and changed no `src` is a loop, not progress.

If SynchronousIoCancelTests.CancelInterruptsACallBlockedInTheKernel (failed once in a full-suite run beside the unserialized repro, message never captured) recurs after the fix and the serialization, is it part of SL-055 or a separate slice?

If a second concurrent CancelSynchronousIo turns out not to free a re-blocked wait, no fix inside the current design can make the repro pass. Is quarantining the flaky test and the repro, with a tracked lost-cancel defect left open, an accepted outcome for this slice, or does it stay blocked until a real fix exists?
A fresh dedicated thread per attempt versus a small fixed set of long-lived attempt threads. Uncontested here; the proposal chose the simpler per-attempt thread.
Cap of 4 in-kernel attempts versus 2 or unbounded. 4 was chosen as margin over the theoretical 2.
Gate and drain as a Monitor-based lock versus a counted event or SemaphoreSlim. Left to the build.
Recording the '>2 s under load' answer as a code comment and slice record versus a docs page or ADR.
The repro stays its own test class with its own serialized collection, rather than being folded into SynchronousIoCancelTests.

No file under .taad/slices/SL-055 was written by hand; index.json is derived by the engine. The answer about cancels over 2 s under load is in the code comments and in this build record, which the engine stores as build-slice-1.json. Delivered cancels: at most 622 ms (spike, 500 of 500). Lost cancels: unbounded. After the fix, the one-CPU repro under 32 busy jobs leaves in 648 to 1565 ms.

No cap-behaviour test that holds 4 real kernel calls (C-010, non-material by design). The finally-block release was covered by review, and the 8-wait test shows the cap is never reached (peak 2, and 3 in 2 of 87 loaded runs).

Other load-sensitive timing bars fail under full suite plus 32 busy jobs, in both the unfixed baseline and the fix: the 250 ms 'Cancel() took N ms' bar in SynchronousIoCancelTests.CancelInterruptsACallBlockedInTheKernel and in CancellationTests.CancelReturnsFromAScanStuckInItsFirstCall (Thread.Start of the scan-cancel thread inside the token callback); CancelAtRandomMomentsEndsEveryScanCleanlyAndLeavesNoStrayCancel's calibration ('0 completed, 100 cancelled'); and ScanStoreRollupTimingTests' 250 ms budget. This answers the design's open question: under load, CancelInterruptsACallBlockedInTheK…

The one-CPU acceptance repro under 32 busy jobs ran 648 to 1565 ms against its 2 s bar (30 of 30 green), so the tail margin is about 22%. If validate's loaded loops see it cross, the test's own single-CPU starvation is the likely cause (all waits interrupted). Pinning to the highest CPU instead of CPU 0 (which takes most interrupts) is a candidate.

Production Exit and Dispose drain without a watchdog, which is the accepted risk of the unbounded drain (O-006, m4). The held-attempt behaviour was measured only on Windows 11 26200. Windows 10 is unmeasured.

Loaded loops met machine-wide starvation twice: a 2-minute test discovery with a blame-hang dump taken while the test thread was still in its pre-Cancel Sleep(200), and one 'Failed to negotiate protocol ... 90 seconds'. Validate's loaded protocol may want VSTEST_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT raised and should treat runs with no test result as infrastructure failures.
Rule 2's exemption lets ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem appear anywhere in SynchronousIoCancel.cs, not only in Close. Fitness has no per-method scope, so review has to catch misuse.

attempts.head: 5654d9b2979db5964482574059927f0595467ba1
attempts.summary: This slice fixed a genuine lost-cancel race in SynchronousIoCancel.CancelLoop: the single canceller thread could get stuck inside a blocking CancelSynchronousIo call once the target thread re-blocked, silently killing the 25 ms resend and leaving guarded I/O blocked indefinitely under load.
